{"input": {"strat_id": "RHAISTRAT-8004", "strategy_title": "Default Vector Store for Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag", "strategy_markdown": "## Summary

RHOAI must provide a default vector store that is available out-of-the-box — without manual setup — so that Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag continue to function when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution image. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.

## Problem Statement

Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.

RHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.

Users expect vector storage to "just work" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.

## Affected Customers

* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities
* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag
* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store

## Business Justification

* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.
* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.
* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.

## Acceptance Criteria

* \[ \] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure
* \[ \] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)
* \[ \] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)
* \[ \] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead

## Success Criteria

* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution
* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience
* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation

## Open Questions

* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)
* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)

## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)

> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.

## Staff Engineer Input

**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that "every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.

**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS="$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.

**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.

**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.

**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.

**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.

**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.

**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.

**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.

**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.

**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. Remove any references to consolidating vector and application storage in a single database, and remove any SQLite-to-PostgreSQL upgrade path considerations.

## Description

Delivered only if the go/no-go decision on the pgvector provisioning approach selects operator-based
self-provisioning (i.e., the dashboard operator modularization, RHAISTRAT-7164, lands in time for RHOAI
3.5). This epic implements PostgreSQL/pgvector lifecycle management for Gen AI Studio in the
RHOAI-controlled operator layer that RHAISTRAT-7164 provides, following the model-registry-operator
pattern for auto-provisioned databases. **Hard external precondition:** RHAISTRAT-7164 must be delivered —
until it is, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where this work can live (the upstream ogx-k8s-operator
cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic).

No new container image is required: `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` already includes pgvector,
the model-registry-operator already uses it as its auto-provisioned database image, and
`RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected
installs. There is no image build, no Konflux onboarding, and no license-validation work in this epic.

Team-assignment note: this epic modifies the dashboard-operator layer (component AI Core Dashboard).
The strategy's Impacted Teams table is part of the Jira attachment unavailable in this workspace, so the
team could not be verified against it; Gen AI Studio is assigned as the strategy's owning team (per the
Staff Engineer input, which scopes this provisioning to Gen AI Studio), but reassignment to the AI Core
Dashboard team should be confirmed against the attachment before execution.

## Scope

- Reconciliation logic in the RHOAI-controlled operator layer (odh-dashboard dashboard-operator area)
  that, given a provisioning request in a namespace, creates and manages a PostgreSQL (pgvector-enabled)
  instance following the model-registry-operator pattern: Deployment, Service, credentials Secret, and
  associated resources.
- Exposure of the database connection (connection string/credentials) as a secret in the target namespace
  for consumption by the Gen AI Studio playground OGXServer configuration.
- Per-namespace scoping: one provisioned instance per requesting namespace (isolation for multi-tenant
  environments).
- Resource requests/limits for the provisioned PostgreSQL, starting from the model-registry-operator's
  PostgreSQL sizing as the reference point.
- Lifecycle management: garbage collection of the database resources when the provisioning request is
  deleted.
- Use of the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image reference (including the related-image environment
  variable already present in the rhods-operator CSV) rather than any custom image build.

Out of scope: the gen-ai BFF side (requesting provisioning and consuming the connection — separate epic in
this branch), the OGX vector_io provider wiring, and any application-storage changes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a provisioning request in a namespace, the operator reconciles a running pgvector-enabled
  PostgreSQL instance with a Service and a credentials secret exposing the connection details in that
  namespace.
- Instances are isolated per namespace; no cross-namespace access to a provisioned database.
- Deleting the provisioning request garbage-collects the database resources.
- The deployment uses the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector (no custom image build, no new
  Konflux onboarding); disconnected installations resolve the image via the related-image environment
  variable already present in the rhods-operator CSV.
- Resource requests/limits are set from the model-registry-operator PostgreSQL reference sizing.
- Build pipeline for the modified operator repository is green.
- RHAISTRAT-7164 (dashboard operator modularization) is delivered and provides the operator layer this
  epic builds in — verified before implementation starts.

## HLR Traceability

- Strategy AC1 (out-of-the-box default vector store, no manual provisioning): this epic is the
  provisioning half of AC1 under the operator-based outcome.
- Strategy AC4 (separate process, decoupled): the provisioned PostgreSQL runs as its own Deployment.
- Strategy AC5 (multi-tenant scoping / per-namespace isolation): covered by per-namespace provisioning.
- Strategy AC6 (lightweight): covered via reference resource sizing.

## Description

Delivered only if the go/no-go decision on the pgvector provisioning approach selects operator-based

the BFF requests one from the RHOAI-controlled operator layer delivered by RHAISTRAT-7164 (creating the
provisioning custom resource), waits for the operator to expose the connection, and makes that connection
available to the playground's OGXServer vector_io configuration. It builds directly against the
operator-based provisioning capability delivered under the same outcome, so it starts only after that
capability exists.

## Scope

- Gen-ai BFF logic to create the operator provisioning request when a playground with RAG is configured
  and no PostgreSQL connection is already present in the namespace.
- Consumption of the operator-exposed connection secret, handing it to the playground OGXServer pgvector
  vector_io configuration.
- Handling of the waiting/error states while the operator provisions the database (playground creation
  must not silently fail; the RAG capability becomes available once the database is ready).
- Reuse of an existing connection when one is already present in the namespace (idempotent behavior
  across playground updates and BFF restarts).

Out of scope: the operator-side provisioning implementation, the OGX vector_io provider wiring itself, and
any application-storage changes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Configuring a playground with RAG in a namespace without an existing database results in an operator
  provisioning request being created, and the playground's RAG capability becomes functional once the
  operator exposes the connection — with no manual user steps.
- The BFF uses an existing namespace connection when one is already present instead of requesting a new
  database.
- Playground creation and update flows surface (rather than swallow) provisioning failures, with a
  recoverable retry path.
- Build pipeline for the modified repository is green.

## HLR Traceability

## Description

Delivered only if the go/no-go decision on the pgvector provisioning approach selects the BFF-managed
fallback (the RHOAI-controlled operator layer from RHAISTRAT-7164 is not available in time for RHOAI 3.5,
and the team prefers this over requiring customers to bring their own database). This epic has the
odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly — creating the Deployment,
Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured and no database already exists in the
namespace — mirroring how the BFF already provisions guardrails infrastructure. It exists to keep the
out-of-the-box RAG experience without the operator layer.

Two design caveats from the Staff Engineer input shape this epic:

1. **Portability:** the implementation must be designed so that, when the platform-provided shared
   PostgreSQL managed via the DSC becomes available (RHOAI 3.6), the BFF consumes the shared connection
   string rather than self-provisioning.
2. **Lifecycle:** the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground
   deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention rather than
   being delegated to reconciliation.

## Scope

- Gen-ai BFF logic that, when a playground with RAG is configured and no PostgreSQL connection exists in
  the namespace, creates the PostgreSQL (pgvector-enabled) Deployment, Service, PVC, and credentials
  Secret using the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image (no custom image build).
- Exposure of the resulting connection for the playground OGXServer pgvector vector_io configuration.
- End-to-end validation under this outcome: playground RAG workflows function against the
  BFF-provisioned database with no loss of current capability and no manual user steps (this epic owns
  the connection-consumption slice for the BFF-managed outcome).
- Explicit lifecycle design and implementation: garbage collection of the provisioned resources when the
  playground is deleted, recovery when the provisioned database pod restarts, and a defined approach to
  credential rotation.
- A portability seam so the provisioning step can be swapped for consumption of a shared platform
  database connection string in a future release without reworking the playground flow.
- Per-namespace scoping: one provisioned instance per namespace.
- Resource requests/limits starting from the model-registry-operator PostgreSQL reference sizing.

Out of scope: the OGX vector_io provider wiring itself, any operator-layer work, and any
application-storage changes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Configuring a playground with RAG in a namespace without an existing database results in a running
  pgvector-enabled PostgreSQL instance and a connection the playground can use — with no manual user
  steps.
- End to end, playground RAG workflows function against the BFF-provisioned database with no loss of
  current capability compared to the inline Milvus experience.
- Provisioning is idempotent: an existing namespace database is reused, not duplicated, across playground
  updates and BFF restarts.
- Deleting the playground cleans up the provisioned database resources (or a documented, deliberate
  retention decision is implemented); database pod restarts recover without user intervention; the
  credential rotation approach is implemented and documented.
- The implementation contains a clearly identified seam where the shared platform database connection
  (RHOAI 3.6, DSC-managed) can replace self-provisioning.
- Instances are isolated per namespace.
- Resource requests/limits are set from the model-registry-operator PostgreSQL reference sizing.
- Build pipeline for the modified repository is green.

## HLR Traceability

- Strategy AC1 (out-of-the-box default vector store, no manual provisioning): this epic is the
  provisioning half of AC1 under the BFF-managed outcome.
- Strategy AC2 (playground RAG workflows function, no loss of capability, no additional manual setup):
  covered end-to-end under this outcome — provisioning is automatic and RAG workflows are validated
  against the BFF-provisioned database.
- Strategy AC4 (separate process, decoupled from OGX): the provisioned PostgreSQL runs as its own
  Deployment.
- Strategy AC5 (per-namespace scoping): covered by per-namespace provisioning.
- Strategy AC6 (lightweight): covered via reference resource sizing.

# Enable remote pgvector vector_io provider for Gen AI Studio playground RAG

## Description

This epic delivers the outcome-agnostic half of the capability shared by every provisioning outcome:
Gen AI Studio playgrounds with RAG use OGX's remote pgvector vector_io provider backed by a
PostgreSQL connection reference available in the playground namespace, replacing the inline Milvus
provider that is being removed from the OGX distribution. It covers the gen-ai BFF provider wiring
(odh-dashboard `packages/gen-ai`) and validation of the provider against an already-present connection
reference. The OGX remote vector store implementation itself is largely reusable (per the engineering
team) and is treated as passive: validated, not modified.

The interface this epic builds against is deliberately provisioning-agnostic: a PostgreSQL connection
reference (e.g., a connection secret in the playground namespace), however it was provisioned — by the
RHOAI operator layer, by the BFF itself, or supplied by the customer. This epic does **not** implement
the outcome-specific sourcing or consumption of that connection: each conditional branch selected by
the go/no-go decision owns the code path that obtains the connection for its outcome (operator
provisioning request and secret consumption, direct BFF provisioning, or customer-supplied
pass-through) and the end-to-end validation that playground RAG works with no manual setup under that
outcome. This epic validates against a connection reference already present in the namespace (for
example, one provisioned by a test harness).

## Scope

- Gen-ai BFF changes so that OGXServer instances it creates for playgrounds with RAG enable the remote
  pgvector vector_io provider (the `remote::pgvector` provider, e.g. via the `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`
  environment guard) wired to the PostgreSQL connection available in the playground namespace.
- An outcome-agnostic connection seam in the gen-ai BFF: when a PostgreSQL connection reference is
  present in the playground namespace, the playground's OGXServer configuration uses it for the remote
  pgvector vector_io provider. The outcome-specific sourcing of that reference — operator provisioning
  request and secret consumption, direct BFF provisioning, or customer-supplied pass-through — is owned
  by the conditional branch selected by the go/no-go decision, not by this epic.
- Explicitly leave the OGX application storage backend untouched (it remains on its existing SQLite
  default) — vector storage configuration is independent of application storage configuration, so there
  is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern.
- Validation of the provider wiring against a PostgreSQL connection reference already present in the
  playground namespace (for example, one provisioned by a test harness): Gen AI Studio playground RAG
  workflows function on pgvector with no loss of current capability versus the inline Milvus baseline.
  The outcome-specific end-to-end validation — that the connection comes to exist and playground RAG
  works with no manual setup under the selected provisioning outcome — is owned by the branch epics.
- Sprint-1-style benchmark capturing the inline Milvus baseline and verifying pgvector is in the same
  order of magnitude — development-experimentation scope, no strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99 thresholds
  are explicitly not required); typical playground usage involves small document sets, so flat scan (no
  vector index) is sufficient for the default.
- PostgreSQL resource requests/limits for the default instance, starting from the model-registry
  operator's PostgreSQL sizing as the reference point and adjusting based on the benchmark results.
- Passive validation of the OGX remote pgvector provider (OGX Core): confirm the existing remote vector
  store implementation works against the provisioned database with no ogx-distribution code changes.

production-scale workloads should use an external vector database).

Then stop.\n23\t\n24\tFor either triage path, write the epic file per Step 8b, then set summary frontmatter and the completion sentinel:\n25\t\n26\t```bash\n27\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n28\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=1 critical_path_length=1 \\\n29\t    triage=below-threshold triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"\n30\t\n31\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n32\t```\n33\t\n34\tUse `triage=docs-only` for Check 2. The `decompose_complete=true` line must be your **final action** — the pipeline will not launch the review agent until it is set.\n35\t\n36\tIf neither check fires, proceed to Step 1.\n37\t\n38\t## Step 1: Parse Strategy Structure\n39\t\n40\tExtract these sections from the strategy:\n41\t\n42\t- **Affected Components table**: (component name, what changes, owner team)\n43\t- **Impacted Teams table**: (team, components owned, involvement)\n44\t- **High Level Requirements**: with P0/P1/P2 priority\n45\t- **Dependencies table**: (dependency, type, status, impact if blocked)\n46\t- **Acceptance Criteria**: (Given/When/Then with \"measured by\" clauses)\n47\t- **Non-Functional Requirements**\n48\t\n49\tIf any required section is missing, note it as a health warning but proceed with available information.\n50\t\n51\t## Step 1.5: Parse Staff Engineer Input\n52\t\n53\tIf the strategy contains a Staff Engineer Input section that is non-empty (beyond template placeholder text):\n54\t\n55\t- Parse it first — it takes precedence\n56\t- When Staff Engineer Input diverges from AI-generated Technical Approach, use the Staff Engineer Input\n57\t- Log each override for traceability in the decomposition summary\n58\t\n59\t## Step 2: Build Component Graph\n60\t\n61\t**Component name constraint:** Read `.context/rhai-components.txt` for the canonical list of RHAI Jira components. When assigning a component to an epic, you MUST use a name from this list. Match the strategy's Affected Components to the closest canonical name. If no reasonable match exists, use the closest parent-level component (e.g. \"Model Serving Runtimes\" for a new runtime not yet in the list). Log any non-obvious mappings in the decomposition summary.\n62\t\n63\tFor each (component, change, owner team) tuple from the Affected Components table:\n64\t\n65\t**Active vs. Passive classification:**\n66\t- **Active component**: Code changes needed → generates epic(s)\n67\t- **Passive component**: No code changes, keep working → validation becomes acceptance criterion on nearest active component's epic\n68\t- **Exception**: If a different team validates the passive component → generate a separate validation Implementation epic owned by that team\n69\t\n70\t**New component detection:**\n71\t- Check `.context/architecture-context/` for component existence\n72\t- Component is \"in platform\" if an architecture context file exists for it\n73\t- Component NOT in architecture context → create:\n74\t  - Implementation epic(s) for provisioning with appropriate `implementation_type`\n75\t  - Investigation epic if dependency availability needs validation\n76\t\n77\t## Step 3: Identify Investigation Epics\n78\t\n79\tFirst, systematically scan the strategy for all unknowns — check the open questions table, risks table, assumptions, pending reviews, and conditional ADRs. Do not rely on the technical approach section alone; open questions are often in tables at the end of the strategy and may contradict or qualify the detailed technical description.\n80\t\n81\tCollect the full list of unknowns before creating any Investigation epics. Then evaluate each independently:\n82\t\n83\t**Decision rule: Does the answer change which downstream epics exist or what they do?**\n84\t\n85\t- **YES** → Investigation epic. Determine which downstream epics depend on the outcome. Add as DAG edges. For bounded outcomes (≤3 possibilities): output conditional decomposition branches.\n86\t- **NO** → Acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic. Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.\n87\t\n88\tMultiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.\n89\t\n90\t## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics\n91\t\n92\t**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n100\t\n101\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n102\t\n103\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n104\t\n105\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n106\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n107\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n108\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n109\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n110\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n111\t\n112\t### Investigation Edges\n113\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n114\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n115\t\n116\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n117\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n118\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.\n119\t7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)\n120\t8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)\n121\t9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)\n122\t10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` (\"the code needs a build pipeline first\") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation.\n123\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n124\t\n125\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n126\t12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)\n127\t13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel.\n128\t14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel\n129\t15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n130\t\n131\t### External Dependency Edges\n132\t16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)\n133\t17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)\n134\t18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)\n135\t\n136\t### Epic Generation Rules\n137\t19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation\n138\t20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).\n139\t21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n140\t22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation\n141\t\n142\t### Acceptance Criteria Rules\n143\t23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n144\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n145\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n146\t\n147\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n148\t\n149\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n150\t\n151\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n152\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n153\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n154\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n155\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n156\t\n157\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n158\t\n159\tFor each epic, determine:\n160\t\n161\t### Type (mandatory)\n162\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n163\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n164\t\n165\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n166\t\n167\t| Label | When to apply |\n168\t|-------|--------------|\n169\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n170\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n171\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n172\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n173\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n174\t\n175\t### AI Implementability Signals\n176\t\n177\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n178\t\n179\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n180\t\n181\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n182\t\n183\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n184\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n185\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n186\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n187\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n188\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n189\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n190\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n191\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n192\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n193\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Strategy cites specific architecture context files/APIs | Unsubstantiated architecture claims |\n194\t\n195\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n196\t\n197\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n198\t\n199\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n200\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n201\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n202\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n203\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n204\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n205\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n206\t\n207\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n208\t\n209\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n210\t\n211\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n212\t\n213\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n214\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n215\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n216\t\n217\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n218\t\n219\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n220\t\n221\t| Situation | Handling |\n222\t|-----------|---------|\n223\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n224\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n225\t\n226\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n227\t\n228\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n229\t\n230\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n231\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n232\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n233\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n234\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n235\t\n236\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n237\t\n238\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n239\t\n240\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n241\t\n242\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n243\t\n244\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n245\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n246\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n247\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n248\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n249\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n250\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n251\t\n252\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n253\t\n254\t```bash\n255\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n256\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n257\t```\n258\t\n259\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n260\t\n261\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n262\t\n263\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n264\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n265\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n266\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n267\tfor the implementing team.\n268\t\n269\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n270\t\n271\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n272\t\n273\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n274\t\n275\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n276\t   - **Title** (one line)\n277\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n278\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n279\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n280\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n281\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n282\t\n283\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n284\t\n285\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n286\t\n287\t```bash\n288\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n289\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n290\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n291\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n292\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n293\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n294\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n295\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n296\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n297\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n298\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n299\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n302\t```\n303\t\n304\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n305\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n306\t\n307\t```bash\n308\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n309\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n310\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n311\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n312\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n313\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n314\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n315\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n316\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n317\t```\n318\t\n319\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n320\t\n321\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n322\t\n323\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n324\t\n325\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n326\t```\n327\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n328\t```\n329\t\n330\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.\n331\t\n332\tThen, as your **final action** — after every epic file is written and any divergence is fixed — mark the decomposition complete:\n333\t\n334\t```\n335\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n336\t```\n337\t\n338\tThe pipeline uses this field to detect that you have finished. Until it is set, the review agent is not launched. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.\n19\t\n20\t## Problem Statement\n21\t\n22\tGen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.\n23\t\n24\tRHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.\n25\t\n26\tUsers expect vector storage to \"just work\" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.\n27\t\n28\t## Affected Customers\n29\t\n30\t* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities\n31\t* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag\n32\t* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store\n33\t\n34\t## Business Justification\n35\t\n36\t* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.\n37\t* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.\n38\t* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.\n39\t\n40\t## Acceptance Criteria\n41\t\n42\t* \\[ \\] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure\n43\t* \\[ \\] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n44\t* \\[ \\] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n45\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)\n46\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)\n47\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead\n48\t\n49\t## Success Criteria\n50\t\n51\t* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution\n52\t* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience\n53\t* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation\n54\t\n55\t## Open Questions\n56\t\n57\t* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)\n58\t* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)\n59\t\n60\t## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)\n61\t\n62\t> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.\n63\t\n64\t## Staff Engineer Input\n65\t\n66\t**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that \"every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database\" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.\n67\t\n68\t**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS=\"$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector\"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.\n69\t\n70\t**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.\n71\t\n72\t**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.\n73\t\n74\t**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.\n75\t\n76\t**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.\n77\t\n78\t**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.\n79\t\n80\t**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.\n81\t\n82\t**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. [source: Dockerfile.konflux:52, Dockerfile.konflux.dashboard-operator:37, dashboard-operator/charts/dashboard/values.yaml:18]\n15\t\n16\t**Detailed**: odh-dashboard is a multi-component platform console consisting of three tiers: (1) a React/PatternFly single-page application served via Webpack Module Federation that hosts domain-specific UI modules; (2) a Node.js Fastify backend that proxies Kubernetes API requests using user impersonation and serves static assets behind kube-rbac-proxy; and (3) a Go operator (dashboard-operator) built on controller-runtime v0.23.3 that reconciles Dashboard custom resources, managing the lifecycle of the console deployment including RBAC, routes, and sidecar BFF services. A bundled Workspace controller reconciles kubeflow.org/v1beta1 Workspace and WorkspaceKind resources with validating and conversion webhooks. Each UI module is paired with a dedicated Go BFF sidecar that handles its backend operations, creating a vertically-sliced architecture where each domain owns its full request path from UI through BFF to Kubernetes API. The federation configuration (in `manifests/rhoai/base/federation-configmap.yaml`) maps path prefixes to sidecar ports, enabling a single ingress point to fan out to domain-specific backends. [source: manifests/rhoai/base/federation-configmap.yaml:15, backend/src/routes/module-federation.ts:1]\n21\t\n22\tThe dashboard-operator reconciles Dashboard custom resources created by the rhods-operator, deploying and configuring the console pod alongside its BFF sidecars. The operator implements a declarative ownership model where the parent Dashboard CR controls the lifecycle of Deployments, Services, Routes, NetworkPolicies, PodDisruptionBudgets, and RBAC resources via controller-runtime's `Owns()` watches. Controller watches on platform CRDs (DataScienceCluster, DSCInitialization, KServe InferenceService, ModelRegistry, MLflow, TrustyAI, Feast) enable the dashboard to reflect the real-time state of the AI platform without polling. The operator uses `odh-platform-utilities` for platform detection, manifest rendering, and deployment helpers. [source: dashboard-operator/charts/dashboard/values.yaml:15-18, dashboard-operator/go.mod:6, dashboard-operator/config/rbac/role.yaml:1]\n23\t\n24\tAuthentication follows a two-layer model: kube-rbac-proxy fronts the Node.js backend (port 8443) performing OpenShift OAuth validation and injecting identity headers (`x-forwarded-access-token`, `x-auth-request-user`, `x-auth-request-groups`), while each Go BFF sidecar independently validates Bearer tokens and performs SubjectAccessReviews against the Kubernetes API for fine-grained authorization. The agent-ops BFF extends this with per-agent RBAC via SubjectAccessReviews for agent-specific access control. The Node.js backend additionally proxies Kubernetes API calls (`/api/k8s/*`) by converting user tokens to impersonation headers, allowing the frontend to interact with the cluster API through the dashboard service boundary.
